content: Cefadroxil is a cephalosporin antibiotic prescribed to treat bacterial infections, including those affecting the skin, throat, and urinary tract. It is not effective against viral infections such as colds or the flu. In some cases, it may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Cefadroxil is available in capsule, tablet, and liquid forms for oral administration. It is typically taken once daily or every 12 hours (twice daily) for a duration of 7 to 10 days. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take cefadroxil exactly as directed. Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not take it more frequently than instructed. Shake the liquid form well before each use to ensure even mixing. Swallow the capsules and tablets whole with a full glass of water. Continue taking cefadroxil even if you feel better, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. Before taking cefadroxil, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to cefadroxil, other cephalosporin antibiotics (e.g., cefaclor or cephalexin), penicillin, or any other drugs. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially other antibiotics, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), probenecid, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease, colitis, or stomach problems. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking cefadroxil, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are taking cefadroxil. Cefadroxil may cause stomach upset. To minimize this, take it with food or milk. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Cefadroxil may cause side effects. Minor side effects include upset stomach, diarrhea, vomiting, and mild skin rash. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects requiring immediate medical attention include severe skin rash, itching, hives, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, unusual bleeding or bruising, sore throat, painful mouth or throat sores, and vaginal infections. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store cefadroxil in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Capsules and tablets should be stored at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Liquid medication should be refrigerated, tightly closed, and discarded after 14 days. Do not freeze the liquid form. Dispose of unused or expired medication properly; consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor may order tests to monitor your response to cefadroxil. If you have diabetes, use Clinistix or TesTape (not Clinitest) to test your urine for sugar while taking this medication. Do not share your medication with others. Your prescription is likely not refillable. If your symptoms persist after completing the course of cefadroxil, contact your doctor.
